looks like based on these choices selected, provider library dependency needs to updated in meson build file as well.
yes , we can basically check for the provider library presence in the meson configure step and bail out if its not present.

Key items for this review:
1. bmcweb should be operating on an interface (ie dbus or the filesystem).  It should require no configurability based on whether a TPM is present, because in the design, the webserver itself shouldn't care.
2. I'd really like to see designs looked at that completely remove the need for the webserver to see the private key, because TLS connection specifics are done in a completely different application. https://github.com/h2o/neverbleed is one example of such an abstraction.  If the goal is to improve security, bmcweb having access to the private key at all means that there's a potential for leakage.
3. Would like to see the design call out the actual interfaces between components.  Today, we have PCM and bmcweb which communicate via dbus and the filesystem for keys.

Hi Ed, Thanks alot for the feedback. I attempted to reply your comments inline. I do believe that by adopting the proposed design the private key will be virtually locked into the TPM/hardware providers and would not be exposed over the file system like it does today and even bmcweb would not be able to read the private key. There were some questions and problems on exposing the keys over dbus and files which I have outlined below, but happy to collaborate & work with you to fine-tune the design to make it secure & efficient.

I wrote a sample server/client app that leverages the openssl 3.0API's and loads the tpm provider to do mTLS here at : https://github.com/manojkiraneda/mtls-with-tpm2/tree/main , this might give a better idea on what i am trying to do.
Done
This design does nothing to solve the "scalability challenges" nor "performance bottlenecks". I would expect this implementation to be slower.

You are right, but this statement would only hold true for certain TPM devices in market at the moment, correct ?

I would think that the performance would be better if we use another hardware for example : AMD Secure Processor, NXP SE050 Secure Element are definitely faster than the TPM and I do think the in future/In market currently there are general purpose crypto accelerators that are just built for running these cryptographic operations much faster, better & efficient than BMC.

Would changing the title to `Provider API support in bmcweb & certificate-manager` a better bit ?
Done

The point here is that the goal here isn't "scalability".  From what I understand of this performance, having to go to a separate hardware component will always be slower, and will introduce a single point that needs to be locked for all connections coming in in parallel.

My ask was that we just remove these two.  The goal is here limit exposure of sensitive keys, lets keep it about that.
Can we be a little more specific about _which_ cryptographic operations and why?

TPM's are built for doing things like random number generation , key generation & key management, Digital signatures, asymmetric encryption and decryption, secure key wrapping & unsealing, HMAC, hashing.

and regarding why :

Why not offload the above tasks from the BMC CPU, if we have better hardware built for doing the crypto operations in much more secure & faster way.

I have added these details in the document as well.

"why not" isn't an argument.

"we have better hardware built for doing the crypto operations in much more secure & faster way."

Is an argument.
Is there any utility in the AST2600 root-of-trust / trustzone-secured enclave?  Would this be better from a performance stand-point?

Potentially, yes -  I do believe that the trust zone secure enclave could be faster than the TPM since the operations don't leave the CPU over an arbitrary bus like I2C/SPI. And I think most of the ARM based SOC's implementing trust zone also include crypto engines on SOC for AES, SHA, ECC e.t.c that might make things even faster.

I am not sure how the trust zone secured enclave works in openbmc & if there are designs out there that would implement it in openbmc. Scaling this design to trust zone secured enclave is a little farfetched idea for me, but I think this solution can coexist with trust zone secured enclave in the future, and users can opt for what they want.
Done
bmcweb should have no knowledge of the crypto provider.  It needs to be abstracted away appropriately through phosphor-certificate-manager.

I agree to your point, a dbus interface to pass the certificates from certificate-manager to bmcweb seems like an easy solution for a public key, but the real problem is that we cannot share the private key via dbus or through files.

In case of hardware providers like TPM, the private key is owned & locked inside the TPM and no one can extract the key out of it. And webservers like *nginx* were using various options in configuration files to feed in the provider info to the daemon. So i tried to implement a similar approach here - so that user could feed in which providers he wants and bmcweb would dynamically link to the specified provider shared library at runtime - so that it can ask the device to do the operations on its behalf.

OpenSSL feature is used my other repo's like software manger etc. It is better to limit scope only for certificate and private key management. Like "tpm2-openssl`: For integrating TPM as an OpenSSL provider." this statement is bit confusing on the scope.
Sure, I added this statement as an example to make it explicit.

This is not a kind of flexibility I'm interested in supporting, given that it's very unlikely that those configuring bmcweb have actually done an analysis of what the path is, and it's a lot more likely that someone makes a mistake.

If we want to select from one of a couple of paths, depending on whether the certificate is temporal or not (ie switch between /etc and /run), I'm happy to see that implemented, but ideally we shouldn't be passing these through the filesystem at all.  pcm can just host the appropriate interface for bmcweb to grab the certificate.

The intent behind this ask is I want the user to configure and mention where the certificates and keys are present. In the current state the certificates are at /etc/ssl/certs and that is sort of hardcoded in bmcweb and certificate manager. And that pem file has both the key and the certificate.

In TPM world, the key is different from certificate & the private key cannot be extracted out of the TPM, so we would need two different handles, one to point to the certificate and another to point the private key.

If we don't want user to configure this - then we would need to decide on predefined TPM handles for storing the server private key and certificate. But this makes every one in the openbmc to ahdere to certain TPM handle to store the key and a certain handle to store the certificate. How does this sound ?
I believe instead of providing flexibility to configure TPM handles, its better to go with predefined or randomly generated TPM handles for storing the server private key and certificate.
Yes, I am okay with predefined handles too. Just wanted to give the flexibility to the companies to decide which handles they want to assign for what purpose.

If all of this is about moving where the key comes from, that's fine, but EM owns that.  I get a little worried when we talk about abstract things like "To enable greater flexibility"

We should talk about what we want to solve, and how this solves it.  I find it unlikely that we really need ALL things to be possible.
nit: "file://" if you're going to call it a URI.
ah, missed it. Thanks. Done.
Doesn't this defeat the whole purpose of the design if the private key is available in plaintext?  I'm not sure i understand how this option could be used correctly.

No ed, This is how it is as of today. The pem file in BMC is in plain text and the private key is in it.

All I was trying to do is making it a meson option, so that user's could give something like 

```
value:['handle:0x81000000'] <- which points to a TPM handle 
```

And by doing this bmcweb would only able to know that the private key is stored in certain TPM handle, but it cannot read the private key as the private keys inside the TPM are locked within the TPM and cannot be extracted out of it.
Done
I'm not sure this is closed.  The goal here is you want to separate private key and certificate so they're not in the same file.  Just keep the existing location as the certificate?

There is one big issue with TPMs and the Aspeed chip that you might not be aware of.  The SPI hardware in the Aspeed chip does not allow bi-directional data flow, which makes it impossible to use this hardware for TPMs.  You instead have to enable the GPIO bit-bang driver in order to use this chip.

You mentioned the performance impact but this decreases performance even further.

> There is one big issue with TPMs and the Aspeed chip that you might not be aware of.  The SPI hardware in the Aspeed chip does not allow bi-directional data flow, which makes it impossible to use this hardware for TPMs.  You instead have to enable the GPIO bit-bang driver in order to use this chip.
> 
> You mentioned the performance impact but this decreases performance even further.


I was not aware of it, IBM uses [I2C interface connected TPM](https://www.kernel.org/doc/Documentation/devicetree/bindings/tpm/tcg%2Ctpm-tis-i2c.yaml) . Yeah it would reduce the performance but its not just about the TPM that this design talks about - this design is largely valid for any hardware device. With the openssl provider framework it is just as simple as adding the provider into the meson option and loading the shared libary at runtime.
Done

I understand you likely don't have code ready for this but it would be good to have real data here.  If enabling the TPM only allows you to do 1 connection-per-second, this is a feature nobody will ever enable.

I do have a [sample prototype code](https://github.com/manojkiraneda/mtls-with-tpm2/tree/main) where I have written a small web server and a client using openssl 3.0 API's that gets the keys & certificates from the TPM connected over I2C - and I was able to get the mTLS connection working in less than a second. But that's just one connection.

But I think the real numbers in bmcweb would be different from the sample web server that wrote. Would you be interested in the numbers on the sample ? are you aware of any benchmarking tools that bmcweb uses as of today ? I could run the same and attach the numbers in the document for reference.

> enabling the TPM only allows you to do 1 connection-per-second, this is a feature nobody will ever enable.

I am a little confused - wouldn't there be people willing to compromise speed for security ? And also in future may be TPM's might become better/faster ? May be instead of TPM's , companies could use crypto cards which could be faster? Since one of the best open-source web servers like **nginx** out there supports it - I do believe there could be community adoption for this feature.
Done
Please redesign so that this is largely removed.  PCM should be in charge of the certificate.  bmcweb should have no knowledge about where it came from.

Sure, I am willing to do that. But there are issues in sharing the private key between the processes that I have outlined above & with devices like TPM, we cannot extract the private key out of it - so i took the simplest approach where the daemon that does the TLS handshake interacts with the provider to get/set the keys/certificates.
can we have TPM file handle generate and host on PCM D-bus object which can be used by BMCWEB to retrieve/replace certificate or private key in TPM2?

> can we have TPM file handle generate and host on PCM D-bus object which can be used by BMCWEB to retrieve/replace certificate or private key in TPM2?

Nope, that's not possible (atleast IMO). Reading the key from TPM provider returns a pointer to [EVP_PKEY](https://docs.openssl.org/3.0/man3/EVP_PKEY_new/#synopsis) structure & also openssl tracks the refcounts to that PKEY structure. I am not sure if exposing that data over dbus is a good idea.
Done

Is there a QEMU model for TPMs?

I know the one for SPI doesn't work.

Yes, there is TPM mode in qemu. For local development I use software TPM hooked to qemu on my ubuntu. But we use the i2c.

Little more information on this is at : https://tpm2-software.github.io/2020/10/19/TPM2-Device-Emulation-With-QEMU.html

```
qemu-system-arm -M rainier-bmc -nographic -drive file=mmc-p10bmc.img,if=sd,format=raw,index=2 -net nic -net user,hostfwd=:127.0.0.1:2622-:22,hostfwd=:127.0.0.1:2643-:443 -chardev socket,id=chrtpm,path=/tmp/emulated_tpm/swtpm-sock -tpmdev emulator,id=tpm0,chardev=chrtpm -device tpm-tis-i2c,tpmdev=tpm0,bus=aspeed.i2c.bus.12,address=0x2
```
Perhaps add both the command line and the URL to the document?
Done
@Ravi - thanks for the comments. I have replied to your comments inline and marked most of them as resolved. can you please re-open the discussion
can you please re-open the discussion - if you are not satisfied with my answers.

I don't think all BMC certificates (LDAP or CA) operations can be offloaded to TPM, I am not sure if nslcd works with TPM handles.

I agree that this solution works for https certificates and private key generation

Yes nslcd or sssd does not have any TPM support. The idea is that the certificate-manager instance that takes care of the ldap certificates can still work with `file://` URI pointing to certificates and keys in the filesystem.

Certificate flow for https:
 - Certificate manager checks, any valid Key's present in specified path, 
  - If Not create new private Key and continue.
  - BMCweb continues the operation as mentioend above.
Acknowledged

There are use-cases where certificate and its associated private key together uploaded into BMC in a single file when dealing with client authentication.
does this design takes care of these use-cases as well?

Yes.this design also takes care of it. we can import an externally generated key as a TPM-managed key, look at https://github.com/tpm2-software/tpm2-tools/blob/master/man/tpm2_import.1.md for more information.

Similar functionality can be achieved using openssl API's.
Is it supported replacing private key?
yes it does support replacing the key, but this looks like an import itself but onto the same record handle where the existing key is present.so that it can be overwritten.
does this design proposed to store only HTTPS certificates and private key in TPM?
TPM devices ingeneral come with Non volatile area which can be used to store certificates. Current design aims at only storing the HTTPS certificates at the moment.
Looks like DMTF already supports Certificate management under TrustedComponent(TPM) schemas.

yes, but i dont plan on using any of that. At the moment what ever redfish end points that are being used to add/delete/replace the certificates they remain exactly the same. Its just that the certificates & keys would be stored on the TPM rather than the filesystem.

Multipel certificates mean , is it included Trust store manged known CA certificate also ? better to keep sensitive certifcates and keys. instead of making generic statement. curently trust store holds bunch of known CA certicates
I just meant, that we probably need to be able to store https server & ca certificates. Not really all the CA certificates. Have sightly modified the statement to capture this.

Manoj and I chatted a bit.  He's going to investigate adding these things in the openssl config, which makes these things largely transparent to the rest of the system.  Overall, I think that's better, and simplifies this design considerably.
